column5: manna and remembered Egyptian vegetables
column6: For the commentary's Moses scene in which a people ask to exchange a superior provision for near food, the wilderness generation remembers fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic from Egypt; it gives the closest Hebrew narrative of appetite displacing manna.

column5: nothing but manna
column6: The complainers say that they see nothing except manna. Alongside the commentary's claim that people can know a provision yet keep devaluing it, the verse makes the recurrent preference itself audible.

column5: perishing food and food enduring to eternal life
column6: Jesus redirects a crowd seeking bread from food that perishes to food that endures for eternal life. His reading of the manna setting makes the commentary's near life versus better and abiding life comparison explicit.

column5: manna, death, and nonfinal food
column6: Jesus says that the ancestors ate manna in the wilderness and died. This Christian use of the Moses tradition makes immediate sustenance deliberately nonfinal beside the commentary's food-and-durability contrast.

column5: Egyptian magicians and God's finger
column6: The Egyptian magicians identify the plague as God's finger, while Pharaoh remains unpersuaded. Against the commentary's Qur'anic sorcerers who act on received signs against Pharaoh, the verse separates recognizing a sign from choosing what it demands.

column5: Jannes and Jambres opposing Moses
column6: Later Christian memory names Jannes and Jambres as Moses' opponents. Its lasting portrayal of Pharaoh's magicians as resisting truth is a pointed counter-narrative to the commentary's Qur'anic convert-sorcerers.

column5: royal threat and refusal of idolatry
column6: The three Judeans refuse the king's command even if God does not rescue them from the furnace. It supplies a Hebrew scene for the commentary's choice against a ruler whose threat reaches only the present life.

column5: tyrant's torture and resurrection to eternal life
column6: A condemned brother answers a king's torture with confidence that the King of the world will raise the faithful to enduring life. It closely parallels the commentary's contrast between temporal coercion and a lasting divine outcome.

column5: short-lived human fire and coming judgment
column6: Polycarp contrasts a proconsul's briefly burning fire with the coming judgment. This early Christian martyr text crystallizes the commentary's claim that an earthly ruler's threat is not the final measure of life.

column5: those who kill the body and final judgment
column6: Jesus distinguishes people who can kill the body from God, who holds final judgment. It is a direct counterpart to the commentary's account of Pharaoh's authority as bounded by worldly life.

column5: not loving life even to death
column6: The witnesses conquer through testimony and do not love their lives even to death. It turns the commentary's ordering of life into a concrete allegiance under lethal pressure.

column5: Esau's meal and despised birthright
column6: Esau eats and drinks, then despises his birthright. The scene gives narrative form to the commentary's warning about accepting an immediate food or benefit while relinquishing a more durable inheritance.

column5: Esau exchanging birthright for one meal
column6: Hebrews identifies Esau's sale of his birthright for a meal as profane. This Christian reading makes the commentary's wrong ordering of the immediate and the enduring an ethical warning.

column5: Moses' choice and temporary enjoyment
column6: Moses chooses suffering with God's people instead of the temporary enjoyment of sin. Its explicit language of choosing and temporariness closely matches the commentary's sustained preference for the near life.

column5: Moses valuing reproach above Egyptian treasure
column6: Moses regards reproach as greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward. It gives the commentary's language of honor, love, and what receives first place a Moses-specific counterpart.

column5: better and abiding possession
column6: The addressees accept the plundering of possessions because they know they have a better and abiding possession. Its paired valuation is unusually close to the commentary's better and more enduring hereafter.

column5: no abiding city and a city to come
column6: The community has no enduring city here and seeks the one to come. This spatial contrast helps read the commentary's worldly life as the near, nonsettled life rather than an ultimate home.

column5: gaining the world and forfeiting life
column6: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life. It gives the commentary's preference for worldly life its sharpest personal cost.

column5: the passing world and the abiding doer
column6: The world and its desire pass away, while the one doing God's will abides forever. This is a direct Christian formulation of the commentary's contrast between desired near life and what remains.

column5: seen things temporary and unseen things eternal
column6: Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal. It gives a precise temporal grammar for the commentary's recurrent ranking of what is near against what abides.

column5: future foundation and the life that is truly life
column6: The wealthy are told to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life. This closely illuminates the commentary's distinction between the named life now and the more lasting life beyond it.

column5: sowing to flesh or Spirit
column6: Sowing to flesh ends in corruption, while sowing to Spirit ends in eternal life. Its continuing agricultural calculus parallels the commentary's present-tense preference as a repeated ordering with a future result.

column5: earthly treasures that decay
column6: Jesus forbids storing treasure on earth, where it is destroyed or stolen. It supplies the material side of the commentary's claim that the coveted near-life goods cannot be made enduring.

column5: treasure in heaven that is not destroyed
column6: Jesus directs disciples to treasure in heaven, where loss does not reach it. This is the positive reordering that the commentary sets against giving worldly life the place of honor.

column5: the rich fool's stored goods and sudden death
column6: The rich fool plans future ease from accumulated goods, but death immediately makes those preparations someone else's. It concretizes the commentary's warning that longed-for worldly permanence does not survive the appointed end.

column5: present comfort and postmortem reversal
column6: Abraham contrasts the rich man's good things during life with his later anguish and Lazarus's later comfort. The scene directly stages the commentary's reversal between present advantage and the life to come.

column5: wealth choking the received word
column6: The care of the age and deceitfulness of wealth choke the word and make it fruitless. It closely matches the commentary's claim that admonition is avoided because another object has moved in front of it.

column5: life not consisting in possessions
column6: Jesus warns that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. It directly questions the commentary's false equation of the favored near life with what gives life its value.

column5: serving God or Mammon
column6: The saying that one cannot serve both God and Mammon makes love and service a matter of ordered allegiance. It closely fits the commentary's account of preference as giving something the chief seat.

column5: luxury now and the day of slaughter
column6: The rich have lived in luxury and self-indulgence while preparing their hearts for a day of slaughter. It joins the commentary's augment about wealth's social misuse to its future reckoning.

column5: sharing bread, shelter, and clothing
column6: Isaiah defines acceptable devotion through feeding the hungry, housing the poor, and clothing the naked. It supplies a concrete alternative to the commentary's linked critique of loving wealth while failing the orphan and needy.

column5: riches and the day of wrath
column6: Riches do not profit on the day of wrath, while righteousness delivers from death. This compressed proverb gives the commentary's wealth-versus-lasting-outcome contrast a sapiential form.

column5: awakening to everlasting life or contempt
column6: Those sleeping in dust awake either to everlasting life or to everlasting contempt. It gives a direct Hebrew Bible horizon for the commentary's contrast between present life and an enduring final state.

column5: all deeds brought into judgment
column6: God brings every deed, including hidden ones, into judgment. This gives the commentary's call to prepare rather than merely prefer the present a concrete accounting horizon.

column5: books opened and deeds judged
column6: The dead are judged from opened books according to their deeds. It closely meets the commentary's image of acts and traces recorded, then evaluated beyond the near life.

column5: grass withering and God's word standing
column6: Grass withers and flowers fade, but God's word stands forever. The verse joins the commentary's temporary pasture and flower imagery to its final concern with enduring, transmitted speech.

column5: all flesh as grass
column6: First Peter applies the grass image to mortal flesh and its fading glory. It is a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's near life as fresh vegetation that becomes dark chaff.

column5: the enduring word proclaimed as gospel
column6: First Peter identifies the enduring word as the message proclaimed to its hearers. Its use of Isaiah connects the commentary's preserved recitation and first pages with a word that outlasts human life.

column5: the rich fading in their pursuits
column6: The rich person fades in the midst of pursuits as sun and heat wither grass and its flower. The verse supplies a particularly close image for the commentary's attractive, short-lived worldly vegetation.

column5: this world as vestibule before the world to come
column6: Rabbi Jacob calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation before entering the banquet hall. It makes the commentary's daily present choice and later fixed outcome into a Jewish interpretive image.

column5: repentance now and delight in the world to come
column6: The mishnah values present repentance and deeds while also valuing a moment of future bliss above all present life. Its two-sided formulation keeps the commentary's preference for the hereafter from becoming contempt for the time in which one prepares.

column5: today for doing and tomorrow for reward
column6: The talmudic reading distinguishes today as the time for doing commandments and tomorrow as the time for reward. It illuminates the commentary's contrast between a continuing present action and a settled future judgment.

column5: Abraham awaiting a founded city
column6: Abraham awaits the city with foundations whose architect and builder is God. It gives the commentary's Abraham-and-Moses pages an Abrahamic example of refusing to treat the current dwelling as final.

column5: Abraham's better heavenly country
column6: The patriarchs desire a better, heavenly country, and God prepares a city for them. Its explicit betterness and future homeland closely parallel the commentary's more excellent and enduring hereafter.

column5: womb, re-creation, and restored life
column6: A mother says that the Creator who fashioned human birth will give breath and life again to sons who surrender themselves for the law. It brings the commentary's womb-and-emergence analogy into direct contact with resurrection.

column5: abundance and forgetting the command
column6: Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the Lord by failing to keep the command when abundance arrives. It gives the commentary's claim that the hearers are not simply ignorant a covenantal setting: fullness can reorder what they remember.

column5: knowing God through justice for poor and needy
column6: Jeremiah says that judging the cause of poor and needy is what it means to know God. It sharpens the commentary's augment that misplaced love of wealth shows itself in withheld honor and care, not merely in a mistaken idea.

column5: Moses and the prophets as warning
column6: In the rich-man narrative Abraham says that the living have Moses and the prophets to hear. It joins the commentary's final appeal to Musa's pages with the need for a warning before the irreversible reversal.

column5: refusing Moses even before resurrection
column6: Abraham says that one who does not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by a resurrection. It closely develops the commentary's distinction between possessing or hearing a warning and choosing to follow it.

column5: deeds written in a book
column6: The mishnah's seeing eye, hearing ear, and book in which deeds are written give a Jewish analogue to the commentary's claim that what is sent ahead and the traces left behind are recorded.

column5: book of remembrance for those who fear God
column6: A book of remembrance is written before the Lord for those who fear him and esteem his name. It links the commentary's remembrance of the divine name to an enduring record rather than a passing worldly trace.

column5: deeds following the dead
column6: The dead who die in the Lord rest, yet their deeds follow them. This supplies a concise Christian image for the commentary's claim that a person's choices leave a trail beyond bodily life.

column5: a mark on the foreheads of the faithful
column6: A mark is placed on the foreheads of people grieving over Jerusalem's abominations before judgment falls. It is a specific analogue to the commentary's developed image of allegiance becoming a visible sign that identifies a person.

column5: marks borne in the body
column6: Paul calls the marks borne in his body the marks of Jesus. Beside the commentary's branding, bodily trace, and face-mark imagery, it gives a Christian case in which a visible mark declares enduring allegiance.

column5: futile ways handed down from ancestors
column6: Believers are ransomed from futile ways inherited from their fathers. It directly illuminates the commentary's claim that one generation's preferences can leave a path that later generations keep walking.

column5: ancient paths offered and refused
column6: Jeremiah calls the people to ask for the ancient paths and walk the good way, but they refuse. It gives a concrete Hebrew instance of the commentary's distinction between a transmitted path that can guide and a preference that turns away from it.

column5: Moses' chain of Torah transmission
column6: The mishnah traces Torah from Moses through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the men of the Great Assembly. It gives the commentary's transmitted sheets a Jewish model in which a received word leaves a living, accountable trail.

column5: Moses writing all the Lord's words
column6: Moses writes all the Lord's words after receiving them at Sinai. It provides a concrete biblical textual counterpart to the commentary's concern with Musa's pages, preservation, and received speech.

column5: Moses completing the Torah scroll
column6: Moses finishes writing the words of Torah in a book. The verse helps distinguish the commentary's claim about Musa's sheets from the Hebrew Bible's own portrayal of Moses as the writer of a preserved covenantal text.

column5: sacred writings and wisdom for salvation
column6: The sacred writings known from childhood are said to make Timothy wise for salvation. It gives a Christian account of inherited scripture functioning as the warning that the commentary says listeners may hear yet set behind nearer aims.

column5: Arabic hayah and Hebrew hayyim
column6: Arabic al-hayat and Hebrew ha-hayyim are Semitic cognates, and Deuteronomy sets life and death before Israel as a covenantal choice. Its own horizon is life under Torah in the land, which usefully distinguishes the commentary's explicitly eschatological ranking.

column5: Arabic hayah and Hebrew hayye olam
column6: The commentary's al-hayat has a Semitic cognate in Daniel's hayye olam, everlasting life. Daniel gives that cognate an explicit postmortem sense, making its life-and-continuance contrast especially relevant.

column5: repentance one day before death
column6: Rabbi Eliezer's instruction to repent one day before death is explained as making every day a day of repentance. It closely matches the commentary's present-tense preference as a condition repeatedly renewed before the appointed end.

column5: human loftiness brought low and the Lord exalted
column6: Human haughtiness is brought low while the Lord alone is exalted in that day. It gives a prophetic high-and-low axis for the commentary's contrast between the Most High and the lower, near life.

column5: first and last reversed
column6: The saying that many first will be last and last first gives a concise reversal to the commentary's wordplay on first, later, and the error of giving what comes first the highest value.

column5: regarding others as surpassing oneself
column6: Paul rejects self-seeking and calls believers to regard others as surpassing themselves. It provides a Christian ethical inverse to the commentary's developed contrast between self-preference and giving another the first place.

column5: seeking the other's good
column6: Paul commands that no one seek his own advantage but the other's. This gives the commentary's discussion of preference as a directionally neutral act a concrete communal reversal.

column5: two cities formed by two loves
column6: Augustine explains the earthly and heavenly cities through rival loves of self and of God. His account clarifies the commentary's insistence that preference is not cold calculation but a love that makes an enduring social order.

column5: wealth taking wings
column6: Proverbs pictures wealth as suddenly making wings and flying away. It supplies a vivid sapiential counterpart to the commentary's claim that people try to reserve permanence for what cannot stay.

column5: ungodly enjoyment of present goods
column6: The ungodly urge one another to enjoy present goods vigorously while youth lasts. It offers a Jewish Hellenistic portrait of the near-life preference that the commentary sets under later judgment.

column5: mind set above rather than on earth
column6: Paul tells believers to set their mind on things above rather than earthly things. It gives the commentary's spatial language of near and beyond a disciplined form of attention.

column5: minds set on earthly things
column6: Those whose end is destruction have their minds set on earthly things. This is a close Christian diagnosis of the commentary's present preference as a direction of attention with a final consequence.

column5: citizenship in heaven
column6: The community's citizenship is in heaven, from which it awaits a savior. It supplies the positive counterpart to the commentary's refusal to treat the near life as the final place of belonging.

column5: daily self-denial and following
column6: Discipleship requires self-denial and taking up the cross daily. Its daily discipline corresponds to the commentary's insistence that preference for the near life is not one choice but a habit that must be reordered again and again.

column5: choosing service over ancestral gods
column6: Joshua asks Israel to choose whom it will serve, naming the gods served by their ancestors as one option. It brings the commentary's inherited tracks and active present ordering together in a concrete covenantal choice.

column5: not walking in the fathers' statutes
column6: Ezekiel tells the next generation not to walk in their fathers' statutes or keep their idols. It gives a direct corrective to the commentary's image of later people stepping into the traces of earlier preferences.

column5: words placed on the heart
column6: The commanded words are to be upon Israel's heart. It provides a Torah counterpart to the commentary's concern that preserved, recited words must become an inward ordering rather than merely an inherited text.

column5: words written at thresholds
column6: Israel is to write the words on doorposts and gates. Beside the commentary's pages and enduring traces, the verse shows remembered instruction becoming a visible mark at the boundary of ordinary life.

column5: formation in the womb
column6: The psalm praises God for forming inward parts and weaving a body in the womb. The commentary uses its birth-and-nearness sense only analogically, so this is an indirect aid for its image of present life as moving toward an emergence.

column5: loving life in this world and eternal life
column6: Jesus says that loving one's life loses it, while giving up one's life in this world keeps it for eternal life. It is an unusually direct Christian formulation of the commentary's preference for near life versus enduring life.

column5: possessions, the poor, and treasure in heaven
column6: When the ruler asks about eternal life, Jesus tells him to give possessions to the poor, have treasure in heaven, and follow. It joins the commentary's chief-place language to its augment about wealth withheld from the needy.

column5: almsgiving and an unfailing heavenly treasure
column6: Jesus connects giving alms with purses that do not wear out and treasure in heaven. It supplies a concrete reversal of the commentary's worldly self-allocation: what is given away becomes the enduring possession.

column5: treasure and the heart
column6: Jesus locates the heart where treasure is. This directly illuminates the commentary's claim that preference is a love that gives its object the place of honor, not a detached calculation.

column5: God alone possessing immortality
column6: God alone possesses immortality in this doxology. It gives a direct Christian formulation to the commentary's claim that permanence cannot finally be reserved by creatures for themselves.

column5: uncertain riches and hope in God
column6: The rich are told not to set hope on uncertain wealth but on God. As the immediate context of the already relevant future foundation, it identifies the false object of confidence in the commentary's preference scene.

column5: wealthy self-sufficiency and unseen poverty
column6: Laodicea claims to be rich and in need of nothing while not recognizing its wretched, poor, blind, and naked state. Its diagnosis of wealth's self-deception gives a counterpoint to the commentary's claim that wrong ordering may survive apparent knowledge.

column5: momentary affliction and eternal glory
column6: Momentary, light affliction produces an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison. It supplies a precise temporal reversal for the commentary's contrast between a present cost and what endures.

column5: using the world as its form passes away
column6: Those who use the world are instructed not to use it as though it were final, because its present form passes away. This closely fits the commentary's distinction between having a share in the near life and enthroning it.

column5: life as a passing mist
column6: James calls human life a mist that appears briefly and then vanishes. It directly sharpens the commentary's discussion of long life, the appointed end, and the inability to make near life remain.

column5: neglect of the least and final judgment
column6: Failure to serve the hungry, stranger, naked, sick, and imprisoned is treated as failure to serve the Son of Man. It gives the commentary's orphan-and-poor augment an explicitly eschatological test of what one has put first.

column5: eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: The final separation ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other. It gives the lasting consequence that frames the commentary's contrast of the near life with the life beyond.

column5: Moses refusing Pharaoh's household
column6: Moses refuses to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. This distinct first step in Hebrews' Moses sequence gives the commentary's choice of honor and chief place a direct courtly setting.

column5: Moses not fearing the king's anger
column6: Moses leaves Egypt without fearing the king's anger and perseveres as though seeing the unseen. It closely accompanies the commentary's Pharaoh scene, contrasting a visible ruler's force with an unseen but decisive reality.

column5: spending for what does not satisfy and listening for good food
column6: Isaiah asks why people spend and labor for what does not satisfy, then calls them to listen and eat what is good. It binds the commentary's food-preference scene to its larger issue of whether received divine speech displaces lesser appetites.

column5: hearing, life, and an everlasting covenant
column6: Isaiah calls hearers to incline the ear so that they may live and receive an everlasting covenant. It gives the commentary's warning-and-remembrance sequence a direct alternative in which hearing becomes enduring life.

column5: eating and drinking before death
column6: In a prophetic crisis, people answer with eating and drinking because tomorrow they die. This is a concentrated Hebrew version of the present-pleasure orientation that the commentary contrasts with a future reckoning.

column5: a rich person's false expectation of rest
column6: A rich person says that there is rest and time to enjoy accumulated goods, without knowing that death will leave them to others. This Jewish wisdom scene closely mirrors the commentary's long-hope and appointed-end contrast.

column5: Torah and deeds accompany a person after death
column6: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma refuses a place rich in gold and jewels because, at death, neither accompanies a person except Torah and good deeds. It makes the commentary's transmission and preparation motifs a direct critique of retained wealth.

column5: Abraham's disciples, Balaam's disciples, and the world to come
column6: The mishnah contrasts Abraham's good eye, humility, and restrained desire with Balaam's opposite traits, assigning their disciples different ultimate destinies. It gives the commentary's Abraham pages, self-preference, high-and-low language, and final outcome a single Jewish interpretive frame.

column5: written song taught and placed in Israel's mouths
column6: Moses is told to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths as a witness. It closely parallels the commentary's linked scenes of written pages, recitation, remembrance, and warning.

column5: a song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
column6: The song will not be forgotten from the mouths of Israel's descendants. This gives an especially close Torah counterpart to the commentary's preserved recitation and its concern that an inherited word remain available to admonish later hearers.

column5: little with fear of the Lord better than great treasure
column6: Proverbs explicitly calls little with fear of the Lord better than great treasure with turmoil. Its comparative formula closely matches the commentary's claim that value, not mere temporal priority, determines what should come first.

column5: refusing to come for life
column6: Jesus tells his hearers that they are unwilling to come to him in order to have life. It directly develops the commentary's distinction between access to a warning and the choice that actually turns toward life.

column5: hearts weighed down by the cares of life
column6: Jesus warns that dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of life can weigh down the heart so the day arrives suddenly. It is a close counterpart to the commentary's present-tense pattern in which near-life concerns obstruct heedfulness.

column5: short fleshly sojourn and the coming age
column6: This early homily contrasts the short residence of flesh in the present world with rest and eternal life in the coming kingdom, treating the two ages as opposed claims. It is a direct postapostolic formulation of the commentary's two-life ordering.

column5: foreign residence and the true city
column6: The parable treats present residence as a foreign city where possessions must be left behind when one is summoned home. It concretizes the commentary's near-life language and its refusal to mistake temporary lodging for enduring belonging.

column5: life and good set against death and evil
column6: Moses sets life and good before Israel against death and evil. In its covenantal, land-centered setting it is not the same afterlife contrast, but it supplies the foundational choice-of-life formula behind the commentary's valuation of life.

column5: loving, obeying, and cleaving to the one who is life
column6: Israel is to love, obey, and cleave to the Lord because he is its life and length of days. It shows that choosing life is an attachment of love and loyalty, as the commentary says preference is more than a calculation.

column5: hearers and doers of the word
column6: James commands hearers to become doers rather than deceive themselves by hearing alone. It offers a compact Christian formulation for the commentary's concern that the listener may know the admonition yet arrange life against it.

column5: daily exhortation against a hardened heart
column6: The community must exhort one another each day so that sin's deceit does not harden anyone. It matches the commentary's present-tense preference as a continually renewed condition rather than a single past decision.

column5: feasting without regard for the Lord's work
column6: In Isaiah's woe, music and wine fill the feast while people do not regard the Lord's work. It gives a prophetic scene for the commentary's claim that near-life enjoyment can put divine reminder out of view.

column5: a deceived heart turning to other service
column6: Israel is warned that its heart may be deceived and turn aside to serve other gods. It provides a covenantal analogue to the commentary's account of a foreground object displacing the right allegiance.

column5: instruction and knowledge above silver and gold
column6: Wisdom tells hearers to receive instruction rather than silver and knowledge rather than fine gold. It gives the commentary's transmitted speech a concrete priority over the material goods of the near life.

column5: earning wages into a bag with holes
column6: Haggai describes eating without satisfaction, clothing without warmth, and wages placed in a bag with holes. It supplies a vivid prophetic image for the commentary's claim that people try to hold what cannot be retained.

column5: labor and striving with no enduring gain
column6: After surveying works, labor, and achievement, Qohelet finds them vapor and striving after wind with no lasting gain under the sun. It is a sapiential counterpart to the commentary's transience of what is pursued in the near life.

column5: Abraham's commanded legacy of righteousness and justice
column6: Abraham is chosen so that he will command his descendants to keep the Lord's way through righteousness and justice. It gives the commentary's Abraham pages an ethical, generational content rather than merely a named ancient authority.

column5: Solomon choosing discernment over wealth and honor
column6: Solomon asks for discernment instead of long life, riches, or the death of enemies. The scene gives a concrete royal counterexample to the commentary's ordering of honor, goods, and what should receive first place.

column5: wealth that leaves its owner before the end
column6: Jeremiah says that wealth acquired unjustly leaves its owner in the middle of life and exposes folly at the end. It closely supports the commentary's claim that a retained worldly gain does not accompany its owner past the appointed limit.

column5: commerce restricted by a bodily mark
column6: Buying and selling are restricted to those bearing the beast's mark. Beside the commentary's branded-foot, visible-trace, and worldly-priority imagery, the verse makes material access a pressure to display an allegiance.

column5: Egypt's food remembered before the gift of manna
column6: Israel remembers Egypt's flesh pots and full bread, calls death there preferable, and then receives manna. Alongside the commentary's Quranic vegetables-for-superior-provision scene, this is a related but differently framed wilderness complaint about preferring familiar food to divine provision.
